title: Inflation and buying power
blurb: Why the same rupees buy less as years go by, and what that means for your savings.
t1.title: Prices rise
t1.hook: When Ravi's father was a boy, a cup of chai cost {old}. Today it costs {price}. Your mission: find out why, and what it means for savings.
t1.define: **Inflation** is the rise in prices over time. It is usually measured as a percentage per year.
t1.example: At {exr} inflation a year, an item that costs {ex} today costs {exNext} a year from now.
q1.opt.a: A general rise in prices over time
q1.hint: Think about what happened to the price of chai.
q1.explain: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time.
q2.prompt: Chai costs {price} today. With inflation of {infl} a year, what will it cost next year? Type a number in rupees.
q2.hint: Add {infl} of today's price to today's price.
t2.title: What your money can buy
t2.define: **Buying power** is how much your money can buy. If prices rise and your money stays the same, its buying power falls.
t2.steps.1: A cup of chai costs {price}, so {money} buys {cupsNow} cups
t2.steps.2: The price rises to {p25}: the same {money} now buys only {cups25} cups
t2.steps.3: The money did not change. What it can buy did.
q3.prompt: Chai now costs {p40}. How many whole cups can {money} buy? Type a number.
q3.hint: Divide the money by the price of one cup.
q4.prompt: Your savings stay at {money} for ten years, while prices keep rising. What happens to what you can buy?
q4.opt.b: You can buy the same, because the amount did not change
q4.opt.d: It depends only on which bank you use
q4.fb.b: The number stays the same, but each rupee buys less once prices rise. That is the part that is easy to miss.
q4.hint: Look at the cups in the steps above. Did the money or the price change?
q4.explain: Prices rose and the money stayed the same, so it buys less.
t3.title: Lab: prices over time
t3.explore: Open the lab. Change the inflation rate and the years. Watch the price of a cup and how many cups the money buys.
q5.prompt: In the lab, set inflation to {labI} and the years to {labY}. What does one cup cost then? Type a number in rupees.
q5.hint: Read the price of one cup then. Typing it to the nearest rupee is fine.
q5.explain: At {labI} a year, a {price} cup costs {labPrice} after {labY} years.
q6.prompt: With the same settings, how many whole cups can {money} buy then? Type a number.
q6.hint: Divide {money} by the new price of one cup, and ignore any part of a cup.
q7.prompt: Now set the years to {labY2}. How many whole cups can {money} buy?
q7.hint: Same lab. Change only the years.
q7.explain: After {labY2} years a cup costs {labPrice2}, so {money} buys {labCups2} cups.
t4.title: Real return
t4.define: **Nominal return** is what your money earns, in rupees. **Real return** is what is left after inflation. It shows whether your buying power grew.
t4.steps.3: Real return is about {nom1} minus {inf1}, which is {real1}
q8.prompt: A plan pays {nom2} a year while inflation is {inf2}. What is the real return? Type a percentage. Use a minus sign if it is negative.
q8.hint: Take inflation away from the return. A negative answer means buying power fell.
q8.explain: {nom2} earned, {inf2} lost to prices: a real return of about {real2}.
q9.prompt: Your savings grew by 5% in a year, but prices rose by 7%. Which is true?
q9.opt.a: You can buy slightly less than before
q9.opt.b: You are richer, because the number grew
q9.hint: Compare the growth in your money with the growth in prices.
q9.explain: Prices rose faster than your money grew, so your buying power fell a little.
t5.title: Challenge
t5.tradeoff: Cash feels safe because the number never falls. But prices can rise, so its buying power can fall. Money that grows faster than prices keeps up, but growing money usually carries risk.
t5.mistake: Many people think money kept safe at home keeps its value. The amount stays the same. What it can buy does not.
q10.prompt: A bike costs {bike} today. Prices rise {bi} a year. What will the same bike cost in {by} years? Type a number in rupees.
q10.hint: Grow the price by {bi} for one year, then again, then again.
q10.explain: {bike} grows by {bi} a year for {by} years, which gives {bikePrice}.
q11.prompt: Why can money in a cupboard be safe and still lose value?
q11.opt.a: Prices rise while the amount stays the same
q11.opt.c: Notes wear out within a year
q11.opt.d: Banks charge a fee for cupboards
q11.hint: Think about the cups of chai again.
q11.explain: The notes are safe, but prices rise, so the same notes buy less each year.
glossary.inflation.def: A general rise in prices over time.
glossary.buying_power.def: How much your money can buy.
glossary.nominal_return.def: What your money earns, before taking inflation into account.
glossary.real_return.def: What your money earns after inflation is taken away.
